topics.name: Legal, moral, cultural and ethical issues

cards: The ALU (arithmetic and logic operations), control unit (decodes instructions and controls components), registers and buses.
PC holds the address of the next instruction; ACC holds results; MAR holds the address to access; MDR holds data fetched or to be written; CIR holds the current instruction.
Data bus carries data; address bus carries memory addresses (one-way); control bus carries control signals.
PC copied to MAR; PC incremented; instruction fetched into MDR then copied to CIR; control unit decodes; instruction executed.
Clock speed, number of cores and cache size. More cores only help if software can run in parallel.
Fetching one instruction while decoding another and executing a third, increasing throughput. Branches can flush the pipeline.
Von Neumann: shared memory and bus for data and instructions. Harvard: separate memory and buses, used in embedded systems. Contemporary CPUs mix both.
The number of FDE cycles per second, measured in hertz. Higher clock speed means more instructions per second but more heat.
Small, fast memory close to the CPU storing frequently used data and instructions. Level 1 is smallest and fastest.
Assembly language and the FDE cycle
Each assembly instruction has an opcode and an operand, fetched and executed in the cycle.
CISC: many complex instructions, fewer lines of assembly, more complex hardware. RISC: small set of simple instructions, each one clock cycle, easier pipelining, lower power.
Many cores designed for parallel processing of the same instruction on lots of data (SIMD); used for graphics, machine learning and modelling.
Multiple cores can run tasks simultaneously, but performance gains depend on how much of the program can be parallelised.
Extra processors that take on specific tasks, e.g. floating point units or GPUs.
Benefits of RISC for mobile devices
Simpler circuits use less power and produce less heat, prolonging battery life.
Magnetic (HDD): large and cheap but moving parts. Flash (SSD): fast, durable, no moving parts. Optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray): cheap and portable but slow and low capacity.
RAM is volatile, read-write, stores running programs and data. ROM is non-volatile, read-only, stores the boot program (BIOS).
Storage accessed over a network or cloud, appearing as local storage.
Consider capacity, speed, portability, durability, reliability and cost for a given scenario.
Barcode readers, scanners, sensors, microphones and touchscreens chosen for speed, accuracy and context.
SSDs have a limited number of write cycles, while HDDs can fail due to mechanical wear.
Memory management, interrupt handling, scheduling, file management, user interface and device drivers.
Paging splits memory into fixed-size pages; segmentation into variable-sized logical segments. Virtual memory uses secondary storage as extra RAM.
A signal to the CPU that needs attention. At the end of each FDE cycle the CPU checks for interrupts; if higher priority, it saves registers to a stack and runs the interrupt service routine.
Round robin, first come first served, multi-level feedback queues, shortest job first and shortest remaining time.
Distributed, embedded, multi-tasking, multi-user and real-time operating systems.
Runs when the computer starts, performing POST checks and loading the operating system.
Software that emulates a computer, used to run intermediate code or other operating systems.
Open source code can be modified and shared, usually free. Closed source code is protected and supported by the company.
Compilers translate the whole program into machine code at once; interpreters translate and run line by line; assemblers translate assembly language.
Lexical analysis (tokens), syntax analysis (abstract syntax tree), code generation and optimisation. Linkers and loaders combine libraries.
Spreads processing across multiple computers so they appear as one system.
Guarantees processing within a time limit, e.g. in car safety systems or air traffic control.
Software that lets the operating system communicate with hardware devices.
Pre-written, tested code that can be reused, saving time; may need linking during compilation.
Static linking copies library code into the executable; dynamic linking loads libraries at runtime, saving space.
Waterfall (linear stages), agile (iterative), extreme programming, spiral model and rapid application development.
Procedural, object-oriented, declarative (functional and logic). Low-level languages give direct hardware control.
A simplified model of assembly language with instructions ADD, SUB, STA, LDA, BRA, BRZ, BRP, INP, OUT and HLT.
Immediate (operand is the value), direct (operand is the address), indirect (address of the address) and indexed (address + index register).
Classes, objects, methods, attributes, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
Attributes are private and accessed only through public methods (getters and setters), protecting data.
Sequential stages: requirements, design, implementation, testing, maintenance. Clear but inflexible to change.
Small iterations with continuous user feedback; adapts to changing requirements.
Iterative with a focus on risk analysis; suited to large, high-risk projects.
Prototypes refined with user feedback; fast but needs user involvement.
Pair programming, frequent releases and test-driven development.
A subclass takes on the attributes and methods of a superclass and can add or override them.
Objects of different classes can be treated through the same interface, with methods behaving differently in each class.
Lossy permanently removes data (JPEG, MP3), giving smaller files. Lossless can be reversed perfectly (PNG, ZIP).
Stores consecutive repeated data as a single value and count.
Replaces frequently occurring patterns with references to a dictionary.
Symmetric uses one shared key for encryption and decryption. Asymmetric uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, solving key exchange.
A one-way function producing a fixed-size value. Used for storing passwords and for hash tables.
Secures data in transmission (HTTPS) and at rest; asymmetric encryption also allows digital signatures.
Features of a good hash function
Fast to calculate, produces few collisions and gives a fixed-length output.
Tables (relations), records, fields, primary key, foreign key, secondary key and entity relationship diagrams.
1NF: no repeating groups, atomic data. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependencies. 3NF: 2NF and no non-key dependencies.
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, JOIN, INSERT INTO, UPDATE, DELETE and DROP.
Ensures foreign keys always refer to existing records, keeping data consistent.
Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Record locking prevents simultaneous updates; redundancy improves reliability.
Data captured via forms, OCR, OMR and sensors; exchanged using CSV, JSON and XML.
Flat files store data in one table, causing redundancy. Relational databases link tables to reduce redundancy and inconsistency.
Show one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships between entities.
Resolved by creating a link table, which has foreign keys to both tables.
Rules for communication so different devices can work together.
Application, transport, internet (network) and link layers. Each layer adds headers to data.
Translates domain names into IP addresses using a hierarchy of name servers.
LANs cover a small area with owned infrastructure; WANs cover large areas using third-party links.
Packet switching sends packets by different routes and reassembles them; circuit switching creates a dedicated path for the whole communication.
Firewalls, proxies and encryption protect networks.
Client-server: central server provides resources, easier to manage and secure. Peer-to-peer: devices share resources equally, cheaper but less secure.
Network interface cards, switches, routers, wireless access points and transmission media.
Contain a header (source, destination, sequence number), payload and trailer (checksum).
MAC addresses are unique to network cards and used within a network; IP addresses identify devices across networks.
Layers make protocols easier to develop and change because each layer only communicates with the layers next to it.
Use radio waves; convenient but less secure and slower than wired. Security uses WPA2 encryption.
HTML structures content; CSS styles it; JavaScript adds interactivity and runs in the browser.
Web crawlers visit pages and build an index of keywords.
Ranks pages by the number and quality of inbound links: PR(A) = (1-d) + d(PR(T1)/C(T1) + ... ).
Client-side runs in the browser, reducing server load but can be bypassed. Server-side runs on the server, more secure, used for database access.
Keywords, links (PageRank), page speed and relevance to the user's query.
Forms collect user input; client-side JavaScript can validate data before sending it to the server.
Integer, real/floating point, character, string and Boolean.
Hexadecimal uses base 16 (0-9, A-F); one hex digit represents 4 bits.
Sign and magnitude vs two's complement
Sign and magnitude uses the MSB as a sign bit. Two's complement gives the MSB a negative value, so binary arithmetic works naturally.
Mantissa × 2^exponent, both in two's complement. Normalised numbers start 01 (positive) or 10 (negative), maximising precision.
Shifts multiply or divide by powers of 2. AND, OR and XOR with masks set, clear or toggle bits.
ASCII uses 7 bits (128 characters); Unicode uses more bits to represent characters from all languages.
Repeatedly divide by 2 or subtract place values.
Add with carries; subtract by adding the two's complement of the number.
A binary point is placed at a fixed position; simple but limited range.
Make exponents equal, add mantissas, then normalise the result.
Arrays hold items of the same type with fixed size; records hold related fields; lists are dynamic; tuples are immutable.
LIFO structure with push, pop and peek; used for function calls and undo.
FIFO structure with enqueue and dequeue. Circular queues reuse space.
Nodes containing data and a pointer to the next node; easy insertion and deletion.
Hierarchical structure with a root; in a BST, left children are smaller and right children larger, allowing efficient searching.
Vertices connected by edges, which can be directed or weighted. Stored as adjacency matrices or lists.
Use a hash function to map keys to indexes for fast lookup; collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing.
Pre-order (root, left, right), in-order (left, root, right) and post-order (left, right, root). Depth-first and breadth-first traversal of graphs.
Overflow: pushing onto a full stack. Underflow: popping from an empty stack.
Items are dequeued by priority rather than arrival order.
Store key-value pairs, often implemented with hash tables.
AND, OR, NOT, XOR, NAND and NOR, with truth tables.
A grid used to simplify Boolean expressions by grouping 1s in powers of two.
NOT(A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B; NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.
Distribution, association, commutation, double negation and absorption are used to simplify expressions.
A half adder adds two bits using XOR (sum) and AND (carry). A full adder also includes a carry in; full adders chain to add binary numbers.
Store one bit, changing state on the rising edge of a clock pulse; used in registers.
Any logic circuit can be built from NAND gates alone.
A + AB = A (absorption); A.A = A; A + NOT A = 1; A.NOT A = 0.
Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and securely, and used only for stated purposes. Individuals have rights to access their data.
Makes unauthorised access, unauthorised access with intent to commit further crimes, and unauthorised modification of data illegal.
Protects intellectual property, making it illegal to copy or distribute software, music or media without permission.
Allows certain organisations to monitor communications and requires ISPs to provide access in some cases.
Computers in the workforce, automated decision making, AI, environmental effects, censorship, monitoring, privacy and the digital divide.
Bias in training data, accountability for automated decisions, and impact on jobs.
Energy used by data centres, e-waste and mining for materials.
Removing unnecessary details to focus on what matters, so a problem is easier to solve.
Identifying inputs, outputs, preconditions and reusable components before solving a problem; caching results.
Decomposing a problem into sub-procedures and ordering steps.
Identifying decision points and conditions that affect the flow of a program.
Identifying parts of a problem that can be tackled at the same time.
Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems that are easier to solve.
Storing results of previous operations so they can be quickly reused; improves performance but uses memory.
Sequence, selection (IF, CASE) and iteration (count-controlled FOR, condition-controlled WHILE).
A function that calls itself with a base case to stop. Can be elegant but uses more memory (stack frames) and risks stack overflow.
Local variables exist only within a subroutine, reducing errors; global variables are accessible everywhere but harder to manage.
By value passes a copy; by reference passes the memory address, so changes affect the original.
Editors, syntax highlighting, debugging tools such as breakpoints, stepping and variable watch.
Problem recognition, decomposition, divide and conquer, abstraction, backtracking, data mining, heuristics, performance modelling, pipelining and visualisation.
Functions return a value; procedures don't.
Normal, boundary, erroneous data. Alpha and beta testing, black-box and white-box testing.
Track the values of variables line by line to test and debug algorithms.
Measures how time or space grows with input size: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n²) polynomial, O(2ⁿ) exponential.
Linear search checks each item, O(n), works on unsorted data. Binary search halves a sorted list each step, O(log n).
Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent items, O(n²). Insertion sort inserts each item into its place in the sorted part, O(n²) but fast on nearly sorted data.
Divide and conquer: split lists into single items, then merge in order. O(n log n), but uses extra memory.
Choose a pivot, partition items smaller and larger, then recursively sort. Average O(n log n), worst case O(n²).
Finds the shortest path from a start node to all others in a weighted graph by repeatedly visiting the nearest unvisited node.
Like Dijkstra's but adds a heuristic estimating the distance to the goal, so it explores fewer nodes.
Binary search O(log n); bubble and insertion sort O(n²); merge sort O(n log n).
Visits all neighbours of a node before moving deeper, using a queue; finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
Explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a stack.
The amount of memory an algorithm needs; recursive algorithms often use more because of the call stack.
Start at the head pointer and follow each node's pointer until the null pointer.
